utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux. May I remind you, Doctor, that the affirmation that you made still applies today.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. I should have asked you this yesterday, Doctor, but were you aware that at the time and to this day the only method available to the Macedonian expert to identify what could be gunpowder residue is indeed the paraffin glove tests with the diphenylamine chemical reaction, were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read this note from Frau Kunovska in her report yesterday -- well, I read the note yesterday and saw that. And I could imagine that is the problem that Ms. Kunovska refers to, the problem that she had. I'm quite sure and believe her that if she had had further possibilities to carry out further analyses, she would have done so, but that was the only -- obviously, the only possibility she had.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And yesterday, Doctor, and in your report you indicated that another way to explain transfer of nitrate particles and in this case, or and/or power residue would be if a person were to be exposed to the clouds of a TNT explosion and you've also indicated that the particles of TNT would be quite similar from those of a gunpowder sort and that it would be difficult to differentiate between them. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that TNT particles burn in a very similar way, and the appearance of the TNT particles, when partially burned, cannot be distinguished from propellants particles. If there is a cloud of TNT after an explosion -- I don't think we referred to that. What we talked about were particles on an object from a cloud of TNT and this could possibly cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And would another possibility to be considered be the direct exposure by an individual to an explosion cloud. Is it another scenario which you would consider or you would judge it too unlikely to be of relevance?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but I suspect the result would be different. If particles can be seen on individuals, I don't think these individuals would still be living.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you one or two question, Doctor, about the subject which you just touched upon, namely, the visual appearance of the TNT particle. Is that correct that TNT is, in fact, present in many cartridge propellant?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cartridge propellants, TNT is not usually used. TNT is a military explosive for grenades which causes an explosion at the goal of the -- so in the -- so TNT is not usually contained in such propellants, from some cartridge propellants.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But it might in some cases, is that correct, Doctor, with some types of cartridges?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any cartridges of smaller weapons which contain TNT as a propellant. It would be far too risky. It is very inflammable and very -- a very sensitive type of explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, in terms of appearance, of visual appearance of TNT particles is that correct that they are flake-like in appearance and they vary both in size and shape. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: TNT is a compact substance that is poured into grenades and it can break into various types of fragments, among which are part fragments which look very much like propellant but it's not a granulate. It is usually a compact mass, which, after the explosion, as with propellants, it can happen that residue sticks on people who have been confronted with the cloud of explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But sticking for a minute with the issue of their appearance, if an expert were to take let's say an explosive device containing TNT that he or she would observe the flakes of TNT, is that correct that they would vary quite a great deal in terms of shape and size, one from the other, is that correct, there would be a great variety in that regard?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. After an explosion, there are usually very small particles of less that one millimetre with an exception in cases if the grenade does not explode completely or properly, then there could be larger particles which result.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And turning to the propellant containing cartridges of a bullet, is that correct that within a single cartridge the particle would be uniform in size and shape. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are such propellants, but there are also propellants with more variety in form. It depends on the manner of manufacturing. There are various forms of it. There are cylinder form; there are forms that look like little pieces of Spaghetti; there are spheres; there are forms in which the spheres have been pressed flat and look like little discs. There are forms that look like dice. So there's a whole spectrum of forms possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, I would like to ask you if -- if this would be an acceptable scientific process. If you were able to collect, let's say, a family of different particles from different experiments carried out and put them together, would it be acceptable from a scientific point of view to compare all of them to see whether they resemble each other. Would that be acceptable scientifically?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visual observation can always be carried out. This is always a valid method of investigation. But the problem is the conclusions one draws from it. Visual observation does not always enable the proper conclusions that one would reach with further -- with more profound chemical analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I understand that, Doctor. But taking it perhaps one step back would there be any scientific value to comparing those various particles as a group and would there be any scientific conclusion to be drawn from the fact that they are all similar in kind?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conclusion as to a similarity between them would always be able to be reached, but it is not a scientific conclusion. It's a conclusion based on visual observation and it is subjective on the part of the observer. So have you to make a distinction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you would agree, Doctor, that should those particles be similar in kind, again, this might be a factor perhaps of not great weight but of some weight to draw certain conclusions as to the nature of the particles in question. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If things look the same visually, there is nothing which would contradict the possibility of thinking that the various particles have the same origin -- or are of the same nature. But that is all one could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But the consistency in size and shape of those particles would also be a factor that an expert could take into consideration to draw certain conclusions, is that correct, because of the fact of consistency?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Any type of analysis brings more knowledge, gives us more possibilities to draw conclusions about the particles. This is obvious. But where are the limits? But I do agree with you that every analysis brings us closer to our goal of finding out exactly what the nature of these particles are.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, you have made the point earlier that a person which would be exposed to the residue cloud of a TNT explosion would in fact risk losing his or her live and/or being exposed to shrapnels. But perhaps can you assist us in that way. How close would a person have to be from the explosion not to be killed but still to be exposed to this cloud? Is it something which is within your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This depends on the strength of the explosion itself. There are very small explosions. If you are in the same room, for instance, you would have difficulty hearing afterwards. If the explosion were from 100 grammes to one kilogram, then it would be a substantial explosion and in such cases it is very probably that those standing around in the area would be killed, not only from the pressure which arises from an explosion but also because of the speed with which the fragments are propelled in all directions from the jacket of the grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as a result of this, Doctor, would you agree that the deposit which is possible in such a situation would likely be very small in nature or very superficial, is that correct, the deposit of TNT particles?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This depends on the size of the grenade used and on how it is brought to an explosion. It depends on the amount of grenades which explode in a certain area, so there is a whole variety of possibilities to contaminate a different site.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I will ask you to open the binder on the tab 3 of the binder which we have given to Your Honour. This is Rule 65 ter 361, it has an ERN of N002-5794. This is the report of Dr. Stein. The ERN of the Macedonian version is N002-5794. N002-5799-MF/2. Doctor, I would like to turn for a second to the report of your colleague Dr. Stein and I'll ask you to turn to page 5 of that report. That's N002-5798.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition, Doctor, that -- would you agree with the proposition that a person or, put it differently, that the identification of particles which could have been transmitted to a person exposed to a reaction cloud of a TNT explosion would be a very difficult one to draw because of the small amount of particle that would have been deposited?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I see, Dr. Stein is referring to people in the vicinity of the explosion and on the possibilities of contamination over a larger distance. It is obviously -- obvious that direct contamination would be less likely and the diphenylamine test would not suffice, but what can also be seen from his report is that the gunpowder residue from TNT taken later would give a positive reaction with diphenylamine. This is another conclusion of Dr. Stein. So there is a possibility that a person who is directly in the cloud of an explosion and survives and is contaminated and has particles on his body, then there is obviously a link between the -- to the explosion. But one must not ignore the fact that it is possible that the grenade could explode and the person could be there at a different time, not at the same time, so there would be no injury yet there could be contamination and this would have a positive result, according to the report of Dr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Let's take the report one step at a time. As you indicated, Dr. Stein distinguished between the two situations which you mentioned. One is the situation where there would have been indirect contamination by a person touching an object which has itself been contaminated and I would put this one aside for a minute. If you look at the middle of the page where he considers the alternative scenario which is a direct contamination by exposure to a reaction cloud, Dr. Stein says this: "On the other hand, if a person is exposed to reaction clouds of explosives, the amount of residue is, as a general rule, not enough to produce a positive diphenylamine test result, as discussed below." And with that, you would agree, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that. And this is valid for weapons used from a greater distance. We are aware of this phenomenon that, or the phenomenon that gunpowder residue can travel through the air and contaminate people. But I think the likelihood of such particles being proven by diphenylamine is not great. I'm talking about a distance of more than 20 metres here. In such cases, I think that the particles could only be proven with high quality apparatus. In such cases, if you did have such apparatus of higher quality, you would be able to detect certain particles.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Doctor, this was the next part of my questioning. The doctor, Dr. Stein makes the same point as you do where he mentioned that if a person were in the immediate vicinity of an explosion, he would not survive. Then he makes a comment about the quantity of residue. And in the last paragraph of this report, if you look at it, he makes the same point as you did, if you agree, which is that a positive result to nitrate particle or to TNT particle would only be possible, as you mentioned, if more sophisticated facilities were used. Would you agree with the last paragraph of the report of Mr. Stein in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to ask Mr. Mettraux to please slow down.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With reference to weapons, yes, of course I would agree with his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the conclusion is also applicable to the reaction cloud, I will read it out to you. Dr. Stein says this: "It would be possible to produce a positive result only by using very sensitive instruments; that is, scanning electron microscopy, liquid chromotography-tandem mass spectrometry, high performance liquid chromotography, such as those used at the BLKA." So the position of Dr. Stein if I understand it correctly is to say that in such a scenario, a positive result would only be possible if using more sophisticated methods, in other words, the paraffin glove test with diphenylamine would not be capable of identifying those particles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about air transportation of particles over a larger distance, for instance, a distance of more than 20 metres, then I would think this is correct. However, in explosions here we would have to take into consideration the fact that the fragments from the shells can be propelled even farther, and can contain remnants of TNT. It is quite likely that there would be gunpowder residue of this type and so these objects would be contaminated with TNT residue. This is not a convection phenomenon but a transportation phenomenon; we have to distinguish the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. And the point of Mr. Stein seems to be quite different from the one you're making. I don't think -- I do not understand the report to suggest that the transport or the transfer of the particle would not be possible within a longer distance. The point that Dr. Stein appears to be making is that if transportation were to occur in such the circumstance, the amount of particle that would be transported would not be sufficient to lead to a positive result with a paraffin glove test. Is that your understanding as well of Mr. Stein's conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are only talking about convection here and the transportation of particles through the air by wind and nothing else. And this convection phenomenon refers to small particles of TNT and the same thing would happen with other gunpowder. The convection is like the movement of dust in the air, and it reduces over a distance. So we're only talking about convection with wind. I don't see anything else that is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But taking the scenario which you just outlined as a basis, would you agree that this scenario is compatible with the further conclusion drawn by Mr. Stein as a chemist which is that in such a scenario, the paraffin glove test would not be capable of detecting the particle in question that might have travelled beyond 20 metre. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this phenomenon from propellant powder in fire-arms, and with regard to fire-arms I must clearly say that a convection phenomenon, as a rule, can be identified only with high resolution apparatus. And Dr. Stein obviously extended his judgement to diphenylamine, but I believe that Dr. Stein will come in person, so you may want to ask him about that in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply to clarify this matter, Doctor, you had not been provided with any information or evidence by the Prosecution indicated that any of the 15 persons whose results you were provided had, in fact, been exposed to a reaction cloud of TNT. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received no exhibits in this case, only documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And none of those documents indicated to you that any of the 15 persons in question had in fact been exposed to a reaction cloud of TNT. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, those documents spoke about the use of explosive devices and that information had to be considered also. That's what I tried to do. If explosive devices were launched in the area and did indeed explode, I think that that fact must be considered when giving such an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The further question following on this, Doctor, is you had no information in the material provided to you by the Prosecution which would indicate that any of the 15 person, and I'm only interested in those 15 persons at the time, you had no information that any of those 15 persons had been exposed to a reaction cloud of TNT. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, if they had been directly exposed, then the injuries would have been massive, if they had been close to the explosion cloud. But I have no information as to whether or not there was a direct position -- exposure in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Another one of the hypothesis which you raise in your report, Doctor, is the one of a situation where an individuals would put his hands in front of him as the person is shooting at him or her and as a result of this exposure, there could be some transfer of particles on to the hand of the persons putting his or her hand forward. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility that we know from our experience. There -- there are such cases of application of gunshot residue on occasions of the use of fire-arms, and the distribution of gunshot residue on the palm of the defending hand can be very much like the distribution on the palm of a hand that fired a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in order for that person to have deposits of particles as you mention on the palm, is that correct, Doctor, that the shot should have been fired within a radius of two metres from the hand, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. Of course the shot may have missed the person, but a distance of up to two metres, roughly, is a distance in which you would be able to observe such -- such marks on a hand that was exposed to the cloud of particles coming out of the muzzle of a fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You would agree with me, Doctor, that it's a rather unlikely explanation for the contamination of 16 individuals. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot follow to what extent or, rather, how likely this scenario is. It will have to be concluded based on the individual circumstances of the case. I was only referring to the possibility of contamination and such contamination on defending hands and on shooting hands cannot be distinguished. I was not an investigator. The investigation is up to the authorities in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you would agree that in such a situation there would be the likelihood and, very possibly, the possibility that the defending hands would be hurt by the fire, that the hand or the fingers would be shot off. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, on the contrary. Why? The cloud coming out of a muzzle is very large, and -- but the bullet coming out of the muzzle or the trajectory of the bullet is very small, narrow. So if you are in front of or sideways from a weapon fired, you will be contaminated with gunshot residue even if the bullet didn't hit you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So as an expert you would regard it as a possibility or as a possible explanation that 16 different people were shot at from a distance of less than two metres, putting their hands forward and that all of them would have been contaminated as a result of this. Is that a possible scientific explanation?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We mustn't speak about scientific explanations here. I'm speaking about experience, about empirical fact collected in a period of 20 years and these -- there have been such instances. So we must take into consideration the possibility of hands being contaminated from or by clouds of particles coming out of a muzzle. But whether or not that was indeed the case is up to the investigator to decide, because he or she would know about the event that actually happened, and in order to correctly interpret the -- the evidence or the traces found, you must take all options into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, to follow up on your point, this information which you say might have been available to the investigator might assist in narrowing down the range of possible explanations, is that correct, for the presence of the particles?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that certain ways of contamination may be ruled out if you know that things couldn't possibly have happened that way. Yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply to bring these empirical facts to the present case, do you have any information provided to you by the Prosecution or otherwise obtained that this scenario of a defensive hand could have been relevant to any of the 16 individuals who tested positive to the test. Did you have that information in your possession?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have such information and that wasn't the request submitted to me. I wasn't asked to do that. I was -- it was my duty to point out the possibilities. Whether or not any of these possibilities should have been taken into consideration in this particular case, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, there is another hypothesis which you raise in your report and that is the situation where contamination would have occurred when a person who is being arrested or detained is put handcuffs or other binding devices by, let's say, a police officer or another person who is himself has been contaminated. Do you recall saying that in your report?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. And another hypothesis which you raised of the same order is the situation where a person would have been transported in a vehicle which itself has been contaminated with gunpowder residue and the transfer could occur as a result of that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have described such a situation too. There have been such instances in reality, and it was established -- it was thus established that hands can be contaminated that way in a very characteristic fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct also, Doctor, that touching of two pairs of hands, particularly if this is done quickly and not particularly gently, is also likely to rub the particles off the hand of the first person. It's as much likely to rub them off as to transmit them to another pair of hands. Is that a fair proposition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Such contamination is even likely in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But what is likely also to happen in this situation is that the rubbing of two pairs of hands would lead the particles to fall on the floor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particles can fall on the floor too. It always depends on the structure of the palm. If the skin is moister or greasy, adhesion will be greater than in a freshly washed and dried hand, or in persons that have very dry skin, with dandruff or scaly skin. This all affects the duration of adhesion. And there also may be protective mechanisms as in the case that I mentioned, the cuffing of a person. Here, for example, the sleeves pulled -- pulled over or pulled up may -- may remove particles from the arm and when you pull the sleeves down again, then the particles may fall down on the hands, or something along those lines. This all affects the time after which the particles would actually fall down.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the likelihood of the particles having, in fact, fallen from one hand either to the other or to the floor or any other part is also the result of the fact that the gunshot residue do not have a great adhesion on transferred areas, is that correct, that is one of the reasons that explains the transfer of particles?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That gunshot residue doesn't stay around long, anyway not longer than ten hours on unprotected hands. But in practice we must also take into consideration mechanisms that favour recontamination. According to our experience, that is a case when persons with -- whose hands are contaminated with gunshot residue, when they put their hands into their pockets, then there will be a partial transfer of that residue to the trousers. But if that person puts his or her hands into their pockets again, there may be recontamination and this must also be taken into consideration when -- before reaching a finally evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And also, Doctor, the rate of adhesion, if I may call it that, would depend on the velocity at which the particle was projected upon the area on which it attached. And in the case of a transfer from hand to hand, this velocity would be quite low, and therefore, the particle likely to fall off. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of such transfer, the situation is no different than in other types of transfer. The rate of transfer is low. And it also depends on whether or not the particles are transferred to folds in the skin or -- or smooth areas, but there are methods how you can reach even the folds, the wrinkles. When a hand is -- was directly exposed to a -- to a cloud of residue and that residue was propelled at very high speed on to the skin at a speed of over 1.000 metres per second and such a case is the residence time significantly greater. But as a rule, the residence time will be around ten hours in the case of normal use of hands, in hands that are not particularly protected or when the particles did not reach the wrinkles or folds of the skin. Then they would have fallen off again, sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, can I ask you to turn to your first report which is under tab 1 of the binder for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be P421, Exhibit P421.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 4 of Dr. Eichner's report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like you to turn your attention to the third paragraph in the middle of this page which starts with the words: "Returning to gunshot residues." And I will read the passage in question for the transcript. "Returning to gunshot residues, these particles do not have a great adhesion on transferred areas like human skin except when the gunshot residue particles are impacted with great velocity into the transferred area. This happened in practice only near the muzzle of a firing weapon or near the slit between the drum and the barrel of a revolver." Can you see that, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and I have tried to explain that a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. And simply to clarify the matter in question, again, you did not have any indication that any of the 16 men who tested positive to the paraffin glove test had been handcuffed or had otherwise been bound with any devices. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have such information at my disposal. What exactly happened to those persons was unknown to me. I focussed only on showing the ways how a person may be contaminated in accordance with our experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you did not have any information either that any policemen who might have been involved in carrying out an arrest or handcuffing any of those person was himself or herself contaminated with gunpowder residue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information, but from my experience I know that it is very likely that police officers who carry weapons are themselves contaminated with gunshot residue. For that reason, the paragraph on the last-but-one page of my expert opinion was actually inserted in the opinion. But I have no knowledge about what exactly happened to the persons in question upon the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you had no information in your possession, Doctor, to suggest that the -- any of the 16 person in question had been transported in a contaminated vehicle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I do not know what happened. I only provided a statement about the fact that it is highly likely that police vehicles are contaminated by gunshot residue. And this experience was also discussed on the occasion of our latest meeting with the FBI, namely the contamination of persons in vehicles and through contact with police officers. So this is not only our experience that I have put forward here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would like to take advantage of your expertise, Doctor, to ask you about another possible mode of transfer or contamination. Is that correct that there exists various sorts of hand-grenades, various types of hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And one type of hand-grenades would use hermetically sealed explosive while some, let's say, less sophisticated hand-grenades would use unprotected explosive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand the terms that you used. Could you explain what you mean by unprotected explosive or protected explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct that within a hand-grenade you would find different sort of, let's say, construction that within the metallic structure some hand-grenade would have a sealed container of explosive while in some others the explosive would be in direct contact with the metallic structure surrounds or that constitute the hand-grenade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at it that way, there are hand-grenades in which the explosive is directly poured into the sleeve or jacket, and others in which the explosive is contained in a sort of a -- sort of plastic bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Doctor. And is it correct that a contamination could result or theoretically possible a contamination to nitrate particles is theoretically possible from the use or handling of hand-grenades. Is that correct, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can never exclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it could result, for instance, from the explosive not having been properly sealed within the hand-grenade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many possibilities here. You cannot rule out the possibility of such contamination. Even hand-grenades can -- even in hand-grenades on the outer surface there can be traces of nitrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, you have anticipated me. The contamination could also result from the fact that the hand-grenade itself was contaminated, for example, as a result of the manufacturing process. Is that a possible situation or scenario?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to rule that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to turn now to your third report to move faster and that's your report of the 16th of April of 2007 which is under tab 4 of your binder. Is that correct, sir, that you were asked in effect to compare a number of bullet or bullet fragments to three guns which had been provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I have a preliminary question about the scope of your report, Doctor. It seems from the list of exhibits which were provided to you that, if I counted them properly, 23 bullets or bullet fragments were provided to you but that you only carried out examination on 15 of those bullets. And is there any particular reason, Doctor, for your having eliminated eight of those bullets?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commissioned to examine certain exhibits. Those were the exhibits BA-1 -- I apologise to the interpreters. BA-1, 4, 6, 10, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, and 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. So this means that you were not commissioned to examine bullets 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34, and 35 which had been provided to you also as exhibits. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not commissioned to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And were you informed by the Office of the Prosecutor that the ballistic material which was provided to you was, in fact, only a sample of a greater collection of bullet fragments which had been collected during the exhumation process in Ljuboten. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not privy to that information. This material was sent to me and I compared these fragments to other -- to other pieces of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you have also explained in your report that there are essentially four categories of conclusions which may be reached when examining bullet fragments in parallel with guns or handguns and you have described those four categories at page 4 of your report, is that correct, A, B, O, and X?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if one turns to page 7 of your report, you have drawn up a table which -- or where you have applied these four possible conclusions to the ballistic material which was provided to you by the Prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And looking for a minute to Exhibit 1 at first, which is the first of a couple of Kalashnikov guns, am I correct to understand that based on your expert analysis there were nine bullets which could not be excluded as having been fired from Exhibit 1. Is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that in the table. Here you can see that the possibilities O and B are to be considered for Exhibit 1. Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine -- for nine of these parts of ammunition. I can see that but could not exclude weapon 001 for them or we cannot provide -- there is no conclusion to be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in lay terms, Doctor, this would mean that these nine bullets or bullet fragments would be consistent or, in any case, not inconsistent with the suggestion that they were fired from Exhibit 1. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot exclude that possibility. And, as a result, we have to deal with this possibility. But there is no particular indication the -- to put in a zero, there's no individual indication here or individual proof here for B.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And turning to exhibit number 2, Doctor, that's the other Kalashnikov weapons which you looked at, would you agree that in 13 of the 15 bullets which you studied, 13 of those 15 bullet could possibly have come from exhibit number 2. Is that correct? Is that the way to interpret these results?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at O and B for the 13, I think that you've drawn the right conclusion, so I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And -- thank you, Doctor, for that. And you will also recall that you were asked to make a number of -- or to give your expert opinion as regard the possible origin of these three weapons. Do you recall being asked to do that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the task was to investigate the weapons and to see if there was a link to the weapons in the video-clip. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in drawing up this report of yours and that's your second report dated 15 of January, 2007, you also gave a number of indication as to the origin or the possible origin of these particular three guns. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If you mean the origin of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And my question, Doctor, is were you provided with any information by the Office of the Prosecutor as to the type of guns and the origin of guns which were used at the time by the Macedonian forces?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had the information that the weapons had been seized in this region, but I didn't have any further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So the Prosecution didn't give you an indication as to whether, for instance, the Macedonian forces did or didn't use any Chinese-made Kalashnikov. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not part of my activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Nor did they give you any information as to whether the Macedonian forces used any submachine-gun Thompson. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the Prosecution didn't give you any information about the manufacturing origin of ammunition used by the Macedonian forces at the relevant time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the bullets, the projectiles, I seem to remember that most of the material came from corpses, an area where there were corpses, and because of the -- and the condition of the bullets was questionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise, Doctor. My question was slightly different. Were you provided with any information from the Prosecution as to the place of origin of the ammunition and in the manufacturing origin of the ammunition which the Macedonian forces used in August of 2001. Were you given any such information?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, am I correct to understand that the only bullets or bullet fragments which you were asked to match between -- well, the bullets and the three guns in question, were used ammunition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parts of the ammunition used for the analysis, as far as I'm aware, left marks, left rifle marks, and those which did leave rifle marks were shot from weapons. The rest of it could be seen by the condition of the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, is that correct that the Prosecution did not ask you to carry out an examination of live round of ammunitions which were found on one of the deceased persons in Ljuboten. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by not shot by ammunition which was not shot? You mean whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whole cartridges?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, an unused -- were you asked to carry out an expertise on unused ammunition, that is ammunition which could still be shot from a gun?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what -- what result would such an analysis bring? Such analyses in criminal technology don't have any sense. What would be the objective of such an analysis or such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if you look at your report, Doctor, under exhibit 4 and 5 of that report, it suggests that you were provided with two bags of cartridges. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. There were cartridges with the weapons, which were supplied with the weapons, and they were included in the exhibits. And normally we do not carry out any further examinations of the live ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in this particular case, Doctor, were you asked by the Prosecution to carry out an examination to figure out whether any of those cartridges could, in fact, be shot from any of the three guns which you had been given? Was it something that was commissioned of you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would not have needed a scientific analysis because it would have been evident from the calibre of the ammunition we had. You could see obviously whether such ammunition could have been used in the weapons present. You wouldn't need a scientific analysis for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you agree that the evident conclusion that you could draw from this fact is that, indeed, the cartridges in question could have been shot from some, if not all, of these three weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. There were various types of cartridges present.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let's look at it first. That's Exhibit 4 perhaps, Doctor. It is a bag contains 40 cartridge of 7.62 ammunition and is the evident conclusion which you have mentioned that those particular 40 cartridges could have been shot from either Exhibit 1 or Exhibit 2, that is the two Kalashnikov weapons which were given to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exhibit 004, if you look at my second report of the 16th of January, 2007, you will see that Exhibit number 004 could have stemmed from number one -- or from both of the Kalashnikov-type weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And what about Exhibit 5, Doctor. Could it have come out of any of those three guns?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exhibit 5 could have stemmed from the Thompson submachine-gun. That's number 003. It could have been out of that weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to you, Doctor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Simon Eichner. My name is Antonio Apostolski and together with my colleague Jasmina Zivkovic we appear on behalf of Mr. Johan Tarculovski. After the detailed examination by my learned colleague Guenael Mettraux, I will just follow up on the last round of his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 2D9.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: It will be displayed for you, on the screen before you. Witness, do you see the photograph in front of you on the screen? Doctor, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see -- I can see a container with various objects in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the photograph please be zoomed in. Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Doctor, do you see some silver bullets? They are encircled in blue next to the evidence sign.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the cartridges there.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you see also a little bit to the left also a cartridge circled in blue? The cartridge is silver. In the middle of the picture, the cartridge is silver.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be a cartridge casing. I can see an object there anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I would now ask you: Can you tell me whether these bullets would correspond, could be used by Thompson submachine-gun which was the topic of your analysis and expertise?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Thompson submachine-gun usually uses .45 ACP ammunition, the automatic Colt pistol .45. And if that is the usual ammunition, I don't see why it couldn't be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I would like to, however, to inform the Court that exhibits 2D33, 2D34, and 2D46 are officially translated by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does that mean you now wish to have substituted the official translations of those three in e-court or are the official translations already included?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The official translations should be attached and this will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Motoike.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Dr. Eichner, yesterday you were asked and it is referenced on page 30 through 32 of yesterday's transcript, you were asked about the use of an optical microscope in analysing results from the paraffin glove test. Do the documents you reviewed regarding the testing and then the ultimate opinions rendered by the Macedonian authorities, do those documents indicate whether or not an optical microscope was used?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't find that out from the documents that I received. I think there was a visual analysis, but I would have to read the passage again. The use of an optical microscope - thank you - the use of a microscope, I didn't see anything about that. And I don't remember anything like that. I do remember, however, that there was something about a visual analysis, whatever that may mean, but we would have to read the documents of Mrs. Kunovska again to see exactly what she meant. I do not know exactly what type of optical apparatus was used because it is not specified here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Yesterday you also, on page 45 of the transcript, spoke of visual confirmation and that that would raise the level of certainty after the diphenylamine test indicated a positive reaction. Is the visual confirmation coupled with a diphenylamine test conclusive evidence that the person actually fired a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. You also spoke yesterday on page 49 of the transcript as to a discrete distribution and that it not being able to determine the nature of the particle because there were discrete distributions. Were the distributions in the 15 results that you reviewed, would you consider those to be discrete distributions?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see, yes, a discrete distribution. And would see that in all cases where the particles were so far from one another that there was no relationship between them. So there is real -- no real distribution. One only sees a few particles here and there, and thus the significance of such a surface area distribution would be even less, we could say less about it, than about a diffuse distribution which does give something optically.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: So in reference to the 15 results that you reviewed, would you then categorise those as discrete distributions present?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all discrete distributions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: On pages 60 through 61 of yesterday's transcript, you were also asked about whether it is scientifically acceptable to consider the results of a group of persons to see whether the probability of a particular result would be higher rather than lower. You indicated at that time that the results of eight individuals as a whole would depend on the circumstances, and you mentioned a factor being if these people had the same movement pattern. Do you recall that from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember we discussed the phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Would it be possible that if these eight individuals had the same movement pattern, say, for example, that these persons were taken to the same police department, or handled by the same police officers at a particular police check-point, that these persons as a group could be -- could have been exposed to the same types of contamination sources that you have spoke of today and yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This approach to look at the material collectively is possible, and one can draw conclusions from such an approach. It's just as valuable to see how these eight persons were contaminated. And from the collection, or from the grouping, one can draw conclusions, both for the shooting of weapons, from a hand, and for the possibility you referred to, being their treatment by the police. It is -- you can see in the conclusions that similar contamination patterns would be achieved and they would all be through the same type of contamination if they were sent to the police station and touched by the police. It is a possible conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, have I only two more questions OF this witness. I see the time. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Dr. Eichner, speaking about contamination which you also discussed today, can I ask you if someone is in an area where there are mortar and/or TNT explosions and then this person was ultimately later detained by police and potentially hit by police officers using the police officers' weapons, could that also lead to contamination?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everywhere, where there is contacts -- contact with the hands, everywhere contaminated articles or gunpowder-contaminated articles are present, for instance, be they the police officers themselves, then a contamination can occur to the person, on the persons arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Doctor, after being shown portion of Ms. Kunovska's statement about the performance of these particular tests by the Macedonian authorities, and this was referenced on pages 69 and 70 of yesterday's transcript, do you still maintain the opinions you drew regarding the test results that are indicated in your report dated 17 March 2006?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions of Mrs. Kunovska or my conclusions, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your conclusions, do you still maintain your conclusions that you indicated in your report?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I maintain my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, you will be pleased to know that concludes the questions which there are for you in this trial. The Chamber would like to express its gratitude to you for your assistance and for having come here from your home. The Chamber would indicate, of course, that you're now free to return and to do so with our thanks. When we adjourn, which will be in a moment, the court officer will show you out. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next scheduled Prosecution witness is Mr. Kamberi and the Prosecution had anticipated that Dr. Eichner's testimony would take longer. We were informed yesterday by the Defence that their cross-examination would be shorter. The Defence also told us yesterday that they prefer that Mr. Kamberi not begin his testimony until tomorrow. He will take the full day tomorrow. We will then have witness Klaus Stein, another expert witness, beginning on Thursday. The Defence informed us yesterday that they anticipate that Dr. Stein's testimony will actually be completed on Thursday. Therefore, last night, the Prosecution arranged to bring another witness on Friday and that will be witness Aziz Redzepi, who will be the final so-called crime base witness in the Prosecution's case on Friday. The Defence also informed the Prosecution yesterday that they believe that several of the future Prosecution witnesses will actually require a bit less time than the Prosecution's recent estimates indicated and that may mean that we may have some additional time free at the end of next week and so that the Prosecution will work this week to do its best to try to fill in that time and perhaps make some adjustments to the witness schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. The Chamber would indicate its appreciation of what appears to be a trend toward speeding up the process of the trial, a trend upon the need for which we commented on quite recently. It will be in the interests of all, especially the two accused, that we achieve a speedier rate of progress and we hope in what is now happening that there is a definite move in that direction. We, therefore, encourage you, Mr. Saxon, to take full advantage of that in your planning of the witnesses ahead so that the total length of the trial can be shortened. We realise that we're in a time of flux and, therefore, there is not another witness for the balance of today. We therefore must adjourn now to resume tomorrow at 9.00 with the next witness, as you indicate. Thank you all very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.33 a.m.,
